name: Agent Database Access and Permissions
title: Agent Database Access and Permissions
answer: Agent database access and permissions is the practice of letting an AI agent read from or write to a database without letting it exceed the rights of the person on whose behalf it acts. The agent is a new kind of client, but the permission model underneath it is the same one the database already enforces for applications and human users. The central question is identity: which database role the agent connects as, what that role can see, and how the action is attributed afterward. Row level security, scoped credentials, read only roles and audit logging are the controls that keep an agent from becoming a way around existing permissions.

sections.body: Agent database access and permissions is the practice of letting an AI agent read from or write to a database without letting it exceed the rights of the person on whose behalf it acts. The agent is a new kind of client, but the permission model underneath it is the same one the database already enforces for applications and human users. The central question is identity: which database role the agent connects as, what that role can see, and how the action is attributed afterward. Row level security, scoped credentials, read only roles and audit logging are the controls that keep an agent from becoming a way around existing permissions.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The agent usually reaches the database through a connection pool or a service layer rather than a direct socket, and that layer is where credentials are issued and scoped. Common patterns include a short lived token or a per user database role, so the agent never holds a single all powerful login. Read replicas are often used for query heavy agents, and a separate write path is kept narrow and explicit. The database itself supplies the enforcement points: roles and grants, row level security policies, views, and query logging. Where the agent generates SQL, a parser or policy engine may sit in front of execution to reject statements outside the allowed shape.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work starts by mapping what the agent is allowed to do to the roles and policies the database already has, rather than inventing a parallel permission system. Queries are typically parameterized and constrained to a known set of tables and columns, with row filters applied by the database using the acting user's identity. Read only access is the default for analytical and question answering agents, and any write path is separated, reviewed and logged. Audit logging records the user, the agent, the statement and the rows touched, which is what makes later review possible. Testing includes attempts to reach data the acting user should not see, so that policy gaps surface before real use.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Ownership is usually split: the data platform team owns roles and policies, the application or agent team owns how credentials are issued and rotated, and security or compliance reviews the audit trail. Access reviews check that agent roles still match the users and purposes they were created for, and that stale credentials are removed. Provenance matters because an agent action may be attributed to a user who never wrote the query, so logs need to distinguish the human request from the generated statement. Regulatory and internal policy obligations around data access apply to agent queries the same way they apply to any other client. Incidents are handled by revoking the scoped credential and tightening the policy, not by disabling logging.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward finer grained, per request authorization, where the agent's effective permissions are computed at the moment of the query and expire quickly. More databases are exposing policy hooks and row level controls that an agent framework can call directly, which reduces the amount of permission logic that has to live in the agent itself. Expect more emphasis on verifiable audit trails and on distinguishing human intent from machine generated statements. The open problems are mostly about scale and clarity: keeping policies readable as they grow, and giving users a truthful account of what an agent did on their behalf.
